selected.name: Information Gain
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment contributes new facts, analysis, examples, or implications beyond stating a position; score 0 when it merely expresses support, opposition, concurrence, or preference without adding usable substance.
selected.rationale: R17 says it concurs with no additional comments, R55 simply supports adjusting fees, and R42 offers general support without policy-specific analysis.
member_names: Acknowledges trade-offs while still reaching a clear bottom line
Engages the counterargument or concedes its own position's cost
Remedy at the right grain, with a reason the agency lacks

selected.name: Engages the merits versus requesting only a schedule change
selected.instruction: 10 = the comment takes a position on the substance of what the agency proposed. 5 = a procedural request accompanied by real substantive comment. 0 = the comment's entire content is a request for more time or another procedural accommodation, with no position on the rule itself, however thoroughly the request is documented and footnoted. Rate the presence of merits content only; do not rate writing quality, formatting, or how well the request is justified.
selected.rationale: R10, R21, R40 and R59 are all pure comment-period extension requests, and they carry card percentiles of .950, .986, .960 and .993 respectively against dense percentiles of .098, .308, .314 and .272. Four of the thirty card-high rows are the same procedural genre, which is the single cleanest block in the slice. These letters have everything a criterion bank tends to reward (docket number, Federal Register citations, precedent for prior extensions, named signatory) while saying nothing about the rule.
member_names: Engages the merits versus requesting only a schedule change
Substantive engagement with rule vs. procedural-only content

selected.name: Mechanistic causal reasoning
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment clearly explains how the proposed policy would produce specific intermediate effects and consequences; score 0 when it states only approval, opposition, or an unelaborated prediction.
selected.rationale: R19 explains how retaining two standards could produce inadequate historical research and brownfield stigma, while R36 traces equipment or power failures to airflow reversal and containment risks.

selected.name: Distributional impact analysis
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment connects the proposal to concrete effects on identifiable communities, users, regions, or vulnerable groups and explains the distribution of those effects; score 0 when affected parties are mentioned only abstractly.
selected.rationale: R14 discusses rural seniors, home-health agencies, patients, and reimbursement differences, while R01 connects fishing restrictions to American Samoa’s subsistence, livelihood, and cultural practices.

selected.name: Firsthand Operational Knowledge
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the author connects direct professional, geographic, cultural, or experiential knowledge to specific policy effects; score 0 when claimed identity or experience is unrelated to the analysis.
selected.rationale: R23 connects 150 days on the water and specific fishing locations to habitat impacts, while R60 draws on Louisiana EMS system responsibilities and practitioner conditions.

selected.name: Traceable evidence use
selected.instruction: Score 10 when evidence is tied to identifiable studies, agencies, records, standards, or cited source material that directly supports the argument; score 0 when sources are absent, vague, or merely invoked rhetorically.
selected.rationale: R24 cites NHTSA, IIHS, BLS, and specific reports, while R49 identifies Wuebbles and multiple scientific sources in addressing species threats.

selected.name: Concrete regulatory exposure, not generic organizational self-description
selected.instruction: Score how concretely the text establishes that the commenter is a party this rule actually operates on. 10 = the comment names the specific assets, products, operations, filings, acreage, catch, or populations the rule reaches (a fleet count, an affected product line, a form the commenter must file, the crop under the restriction), so the exposure is checkable from the text alone. 5 = an affected-industry claim is asserted only in general terms. 0 = identity is conveyed solely by mission statement, membership counts, or a roster of affiliates, with no link drawn between who the commenter is and what the rule does to them. Judge only the linkage between identity and rule; do not reward prestige, org size, or professional letterhead.
selected.rationale: R52 states the NPRM affects twenty-one of United's own 747-400s; R27 is Boeing concurring on an AD against parts on its own airframe; R50 is a grower writing from inside the exact volume restriction; R11 is Sanofi naming the insulin products that transition under the provision. All four are dense-high and card-low. On the other side R15 and R33 spend their visible text on rosters and mission statements without connecting the entity to any operative effect, and both are card-high. A bank that scores affiliation rather than exposure would over-credit R15/R33 and under-credit R27/R52.
member_names: Concrete regulatory exposure, not generic organizational self-description

selected.name: Written for this docket versus repurposed campaign or marketing copy
selected.instruction: 10 = the prose is addressed to the decisionmaker in this proceeding and could not be lifted intact from another context: it names the rule, addresses the agency, and its register is that of a submission. 5 = docket-aware but partly templated. 0 = the text is evidently written for another audience and pasted in, marked by second-person consumer address, headline-style openers, action-alert urgency in the close, rhetorical questions repeated verbatim, or no addressee at all. Judge the genre of the writing only, never the position taken or the sincerity of the writer.
selected.rationale: R04 opens 'Dads, you wouldn't knowingly bring poison into your home' and repeats its 90-ppm rhetorical question verbatim, a distributed advocacy article rather than a comment, at dense .147 / card .811; R16 closes with 'There's no time to waste. Please act swiftly', at dense .023 / card .929; R02 opens with petition language, at dense .031 / card .910. All three carry real numbers and clean prose, which is exactly why a criterion bank scores them high while the dense model does not.
member_names: Written for this docket versus repurposed campaign or marketing copy

selected.name: Brevity that resolves to a clear disposition from a positioned party
selected.instruction: 10 = a short comment states an unambiguous disposition (concur, oppose, withdraw, support the adjustment, take no action) from someone whose position on that question is itself information the agency needs. 5 = a clear disposition from a party with no particular standing on it. 0 = short and non-committal, or long with the disposition never stated or buried past the point of recovery. Never penalize brevity as such; penalize only the absence of a recoverable position.
selected.rationale: R27 is three lines from Boeing concurring with an AD on its own aircraft (dense .947 / card .177); R52 is United concurring with a fleet of twenty-one affected airplanes (dense .898 / card .173); R49, R31 and R46 are all two to four sentences with a plain position and sit at dense .726, .741 and .748 against card .018, .046 and .075. Any bank with length, structure or elaboration terms will floor these five. R15 and R05 show the inverse failure, long documents whose position is vague or arrives after pages of recitation.
member_names: Brevity that resolves to a clear disposition from a positioned party

selected.name: Interest disclosed, and the argument survives the interest
selected.instruction: 10 = the commenter's own benefit from the requested outcome is visible in the text, and the argument still rests on reasons that would hold for someone who did not get that benefit. 5 = interest visible, argument partly independent. 0 = the entire content of the argument is that the outcome would be good for the commenter, the commenter's program, or the commenter's accreditation framework, restated in public-interest language. Score disclosure and independence jointly: an undisclosed benefit driving the whole argument scores 0 even when the writing is polished.
selected.rationale: R24 is an accreditation body urging USDA to rely on the ILAC/IAF framework of which it is a recognized member; R19 is a breeder whose income depends on the species not being listed, arguing from captive abundance; R32 and R51 are grantees urging extension of the grants that fund them. Card scores them .768, .739, .932 and .869 while dense scores .058, .116, .314 and .210. R07, by contrast, concedes that recreational fishermen should share the burden of overfishing rules before asking for the closure, and is dense .646 / card .057.
member_names: Interest disclosed, and the argument survives the interest

selected.name: Decisive, unambiguous stated position
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment takes a clear, unambiguous stance (support, oppose, or a specific requested change) rather than only posing open questions or expressing unresolved uncertainty. 10 = an unambiguous position is stated. 0 = the comment consists entirely of questions or non-committal musing with no stated position.
selected.rationale: R21 ('We urge National Marine Fisheries to take NO action... keeping the habitat management area CLOSED') and R13 (clear endorsement of the carrot-grading proposal with a stated reason) are both dense_high (.871, .741)/card_low. R20 is entirely a list of unanswered questions with no position taken, and is dense_low (.031)/card_high (.656).

selected.name: Stated expertise is used to generate a specific insight, not just asserted
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the commenter's stated credential, role, or experience is actually put to work to produce a specific, non-obvious technical judgment, rather than the credential being asserted while the rest of the comment stays at the level of generic support or opposition. 10 = credential is stated and clearly generates a specific technical point a lay commenter could not have made. 0 = a credential/affiliation is stated but the substantive content that follows is generic and could have been written by anyone.
selected.rationale: R08's Director of AS-DMWR uses his position to produce a specific jurisdictional argument (federal-water closures alone won't reduce nearshore catch) and specific comparative catch data; dense .959/card .142. R43 uses stated methodological expertise to interrogate FARS undercounting with named correction factors; dense .938/card .249. By contrast R54 opens with extensive credentials (accredited since 1979, ISO/IEC 17025 competence) but the visible argument mainly restates a preference for an existing framework without a comparably distinct technical insight, and is dense_low (.023) despite card_high (.768).
member_names: Stated expertise is used to generate a specific insight, not just asserted

selected.name: Net information flow: contributes to the record or draws from it
selected.instruction: 10 = the comment is overwhelmingly a contribution, putting evidence, analysis, or a defensible position into the record for the agency to use. 5 = balanced. 0 = the comment is overwhelmingly a demand on the agency: it asks the agency to explain, list, confirm, clarify, define, or supply things, without supplying anything itself. Count questions and requests for agency-produced material on the 0 side and facts, reasoning, and stated positions on the 10 side. A question that embeds the answer counts as a contribution.
selected.rationale: R58 is page-by-page requests directed at the agency (provide a list of specific components, what proof is acceptable) and sits at dense .008, the lowest in the slice, against card .845; R55 is three bare questions with Federal Register links at dense .031 / card .656; R23 asks the IRS to confirm reliance at dense .023 / card .768. Against these, R08 and R44 put a fifty-year documentary record and territorial catch data into the record and are dense .964 and .959. Interrogative specificity looks like engagement to a criterion bank but is net extraction.
member_names: Net information flow: contributes to the record or draws from it

selected.name: Temporal and comparative context
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the comment uses historical developments, prior rules, trends, or comparisons to clarify why the present proposal matters; score 0 when it provides no temporal or comparative context.
selected.rationale: R24 compares decades of agency awareness with later technical studies, while R53 compares the proposed comment period with durations used for earlier complex proceedings.

selected.name: Explicit causal chain from fact to recommended consequence
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 on whether the comment explicitly connects a specific factual claim to a specific consequence for the decision via a stated causal or logical mechanism, rather than listing facts, questions, or citations without tying them into an argument. 10 = a clear 'because X, therefore Y should happen' chain is spelled out. 0 = facts or questions are listed with no connecting logic to a recommendation.
selected.rationale: R23 explicitly reasons that because neonicotinoids are 'highly water soluble' they 'travel in soil, water' and therefore 'should be regulated' -- dense .748/card .075. R20, by contrast, is a list of unanswered process questions with no connecting argument to a recommendation, and is dense_low (.031)/card_high (.656).
member_names: Explicit causal chain from fact to recommended consequence

selected.name: Submission artifact markers
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains transmission or ingestion artifacts such as attachment placeholders, email headers, fax details, file names, upload notices, or archived-message metadata; do not judge whether these artifacts help or hurt the comment.
selected.rationale: Different submission channels and docket-ingestion routines can leave machine-readable traces unrelated to argument content. Examples include R02 and R19.

selected.name: Overall length and verbosity of the submission
selected.instruction: On a scale of 0 (extremely terse, a sentence or two) to 10 (very long, multi-page with extensive elaboration), rate how much text volume this comment contains. Score the sheer AMOUNT of text present, not whether the length is appropriate or whether the content in it is good.
selected.rationale: Terse one-line concurrences (R03: 'Concur, no additional comments will be forthcoming' -- dense_pct=.947, card_pct=.177) sit at the opposite length extreme from long multi-page letters with extensive elaboration and footnotes (R05: multi-page Covered California letter -- dense_pct=.183, card_pct=.842). Because the scorecard aggregates many separately-scored criteria, longer text simply has more surface area to accumulate points, independent of whether the underlying position is sound.
member_names: Overall length and verbosity of the submission

selected.name: OCR and scan-degradation noise
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the density of character-level corruption typical of a document that was faxed or paper-scanned and then passed through optical character recognition. Count: lookalike letter substitutions ('VVildlife' for 'Wildlife', 'ltr/ater' for 'Water', 'Ambient' rendered 'Ambient' with stray accents, 'Criterion' fused to the next word); stray spaces inside numbers and words ('(3 17) 592-46 16', 'Page2', 'August18,2017'); runs of punctuation or symbol garbage; mangled email addresses or URLs; and unreadable renderings of signatures, logos or letterhead art. 0 = clean digital text throughout; 5 = scattered corruption, a few lines affected; 10 = corruption in most lines. Judge only how much corruption is visible. Do NOT treat corruption as evidence of carelessness, low resources, age or standing, and do NOT judge whether it is good or bad.
selected.rationale: R05 renders direct-dial numbers as '(3 17) 592-46 16' and an email as 'marc.sciscoeiGlicemiller.com'; R10 has 'ltr/ater Quality', 'Criterion' fused to a following word, 'V/orks' and 'Inigated'; R40 prints 'VVildEarth' and 'VVildlife' throughout; R28 opens on a line of symbol garbage; R57 ends in an unreadable signature scrawl; R58 has whole board-roster lines destroyed. The corruption is produced by the route the paper travelled and by the docket's own imaging, not by the commenter's reasoning, and it appears on both sides of this slice (R05, R10, R28, R40 alongside R57, R58). It nevertheless makes a document read as either garbled or crisp, and both a text-reading model and any keyword-matching criterion will respond to that.
member_names: Density of OCR/scan garbling and corrupted characters
selected.upstream_parent: document-production and submission medium (fax or paper scan versus a native electronic file)
upstream_parent_all_members: document-production and submission medium (fax or paper scan versus a native electronic file)

selected.name: Coalition breadth
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text names multiple joint commenters, member organizations, represented constituencies, or broad organizational networks; do not judge whether the coalition is representative, important, or persuasive.
selected.rationale: Networked organizations can generate distinctive group-signaling language and may also pool expertise that improves substantive work. This fingerprint is evident in R16 and R58.

selected.name: Timing and urgency cues
selected.instruction: How much does the text explicitly mention deadlines, extensions, recent events, production or submission dates, delay, urgency, or requests for swift action? Score only the extent from 0–10; do not judge whether the timing or urgency is justified or good.
selected.rationale: Timing can influence presentation and available preparation while also affecting substantive completeness. Explicit extension and deadline cues appear in R02, R22, and R26.
selected.upstream_parent: submission timing and available preparation time
upstream_parent_all_members: submission timing and available preparation time

selected.name: Boilerplate language
selected.instruction: How much of the text consists of stock openings, closings, recurring organizational descriptions, formulaic requests, or repeated passages? Score only the extent from 0–10; do not judge whether the boilerplate is appropriate or good.
selected.rationale: Coordinated communications can produce recurring language that is predictive of reception while adding no independent substantive signal. Repeated organizational wording appears across R10 and R34, and duplicated template material appears in R52.

selected.name: Recitation of the submitter organization's size or market share
selected.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no mention of the submitting organization's membership count, revenue, or market share) to 10 (the text prominently recites such statistics, e.g. member counts, dollar figures, or percentage market share), rate how much of the text is devoted to this kind of self-credentialing. Do not judge whether the organization's scale is actually relevant to its argument.
selected.rationale: (a) A well-resourced trade association can devote more staff time to producing a comment and also has an incentive to remind the reader of its scale/legitimacy. (b) That incentive leaves a visible textual fingerprint: a stock paragraph reciting membership counts and market statistics. (c) R07 (NAMIC: '1,500 member companies... $323 billion in annual premiums... 67 percent of homeowners...') and R13 (State Farm: '40 million active automobile insurance policies... 19,400 agents... 53,000 employees') both open with this credential recitation and both land dense_high_card_low (R07: dense=.924/card=.050; R13: dense=.835/card=.086), consistent with the dense model being swayed by apparent institutional authority independent of argument content. Tagged mixed because a genuinely larger, better-resourced organization may also produce genuinely more substantive comments, so this factor could be doing double duty.
member_names: Recitation of the submitter organization's size or market share
upstream_parent_all_members: institutional standing and reputational capital of the submitting organization

selected.name: Personal and local grounding
selected.instruction: How much does the text contain first-person experience, personal role descriptions, local residence, place-specific activity, or direct involvement with the affected subject? Score only the extent from 0–10; do not judge whether the experience makes the comment good.
selected.rationale: Direct experience may both influence reception and contribute genuinely relevant knowledge, so this belongs in a sensitivity band. Personal or local grounding appears in R05, R25, and R27.

selected.name: Institutional status cues
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text explicitly signals institutional office, executive or professional title, organizational scale, credentials, or official capacity; do not judge whether any signal is good, relevant, or deserved.
selected.rationale: Senior or well-resourced institutions may receive systematic text-processing advantages, while also having more capacity to produce genuinely substantive comments. This fingerprint appears in the official titles and institutional descriptions in R01 and R04.

selected.name: Signatory's seniority title paired with a direct personal contact line
selected.instruction: On a scale of 0 (no named signatory, or a signatory with no title/direct contact info given) to 10 (the letter closes with a named signatory carrying a senior title -- e.g. Executive Director, Vice President, Senior Manager -- plus a direct personal phone/fax/email), rate how much of this signature-block signaling is present. Do not judge whether the signatory's seniority makes their argument more correct.
selected.rationale: (a) More senior staff are more likely to personally sign a comment on a politically or commercially important docket, and their offices are more likely to list direct contact lines. (b) That seniority leaves a fingerprint in the signature block: title plus direct phone/fax. (c) R03 (Boeing: 'Erica Graham, Senior Manager, Airplane Safety Engineering' with direct phone (425) 239-3247 and fax) and R10 (AIA: 'Ali Bahrami, Vice President, Civil Aviation') both carry this senior-title-plus-direct-contact signature, yet land in different quadrants (R03 dense_high_card_low dense=.947/card=.177; R10 dense_low_card_high dense=.173/card=.957), again suggesting this is a cross-cutting fingerprint rather than a marker of genuine substance. Tagged mixed because more senior signatories may also, on average, bring genuinely more authoritative technical input.
member_names: Signatory's seniority title paired with a direct personal contact line
